claims.text: In equiatomic single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys, lattice distortion quantified by atomic size mismatch parameter δ governs hardness and yield strength.
Lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion through solid-solution strengthening.
The proposed comparison uses as-cast or homogenized, single-phase equiatomic FCC HEAs with grain size controlled near 20 µm.

A five-alloy series can vary δ from approximately 1% to 6% by replacing one of five equiatomic elements with atoms of different sizes while holding valence electron concentration, processing, and grain size constant.
Mechanical testing will be performed at room temperature after annealing to remove residual stress, with matched cold-work history and oxygen content below 100 ppm.
Lattice distortion represented by δ can be measured using X-ray diffraction peak broadening and atomic pair distribution function analysis.
Increasing δ increases local stress-field heterogeneity around solute atoms.
Greater local stress-field heterogeneity increases the critical resolved shear stress required for dislocation glide.
The increased resistance to dislocation glide strengthens the alloy.
Nanoindentation hardness and 0.2% tensile yield strength increase approximately linearly with δ over the proposed range.
Yield strength increases by approximately 50–80 MPa for each one-percentage-point increase in δ up to δ of about 6%.
An equiatomic FCC HEA with δ near 3% has approximately 3 GPa hardness.
An equiatomic FCC HEA with δ near 3% has approximately 500 MPa yield strength.
The proposed δ-strength relationship holds for single-phase FCC HEAs with δ between approximately 1% and 6%.
Above δ of approximately 6%, intermetallic phases or excessive short-range order may form and invalidate the linear strength trend.
Residual microsegregation or minor stacking-fault-energy differences may cause the strengthening magnitude per unit δ to vary by about ±20%.
A controlled comparison of two alloys with δ near 4% but different secondary parameters can test whether δ alone determines hardness and strength.
A hardness or yield-strength difference greater than 10% between alloys having equal δ would falsify the claim that lattice distortion alone governs strengthening.
